question.prompt: In the year \(2001,\) the United States will host the International Mathematical Olympiad. Let \(I,\) \(M,\) and \(O\) be distinct positive integers such that the product \(I \cdot M \cdot O = 2001.\) What is the largest possible value of the sum \(I + M + O?\)

solutions.explanation:
Factoring the product makes it possible to list every allowed triple:
\[
2001=3\cdot667=3\cdot23\cdot29.
\]
These are three distinct prime factors. Since rearranging \(I,M,O\) changes neither their product nor their sum, list each triple in increasing order.

If one integer is \(1\), distinctness prevents another from being \(1\). The other two integers must split the three prime factors into two nonempty groups. Choosing the prime that stands alone gives exactly
\[
(1,3,667),\quad(1,23,87),\quad(1,29,69).
\]
If none of the integers is \(1\), each must contain at least one prime factor. There are exactly three prime factors available, so the only increasing triple is \((3,23,29)\). These cases cover every possibility without repeating a rearrangement.

Their sums are
\[
\begin{aligned}
1+3+667&=671,\\
1+23+87&=111,\\
1+29+69&=99,\\
3+23+29&=55.
\end{aligned}
\]
The largest possible sum is \(\boxed{671}\), attained by the distinct integers \(1,3,667\), so the answer is \(\text{E}\).

Bound the sum using sorted factors
